interactions.label: Layout
interactions.teaches: Seeing the two identical crystals side by side makes the plane orientation the only changing feature: the same cubic lattice contains different families of parallel atomic planes.

interactions.label: Plane family in single-lattice view

interactions.label: Measurement aids
interactions.teaches: Turning aids on connects each plane family to its spacing; turning them off restores the source-faithful textbook view without labels, arrows, halos, or extra emphasis.
Rotating the view reveals that the teal regions are flat planes passing through a three-dimensional atom array rather than colored patches on a 2D drawing.

demo_steps.title: Source-like comparison
demo_steps.narration: The figure opens as two matching lattices side by side, like the source. The left crystal shows a face-parallel sheet through the middle atoms, while the right crystal shows a set of parallel diagonal sheets through the same kind of lattice.

demo_steps.title: Add the hidden measurement idea
demo_steps.narration: With aids turned on, labels and spacing arrows explain what the source implies: each family has a characteristic interplanar spacing relevant to diffraction.

demo_steps.title: Isolate the {100} family
demo_steps.narration: In the single-lattice view, the {100} plane is a square sheet parallel to a cube face and passes through one complete middle layer of atoms.

demo_steps.title: Isolate the {110} family
demo_steps.narration: Switching to {110} keeps the atom positions fixed but rotates the family of planes diagonally through the cube. The parallel diagonal planes are closer together than the face-parallel {100} planes.

plan.geometry_notes: Use two identical simple-cubic lattices by default, matching the original two-panel comparison. Each lattice is a 3 × 3 × 3 array of atom centers at local coordinates x,y,z ∈ {-1, 0, 1}, lattice spacing a = 1, cube extent 2 × 2 × 2 world units. Place the left lattice group centered near world x = -1.65 and the right lattice group centered near world x = +1.65, with both at the same y,z and using the same camera/view orientation. Red atoms: spheres radius 0.095–0.11, glossy red #d71920 with small white specular highlight. Rods: black #111111 cylinders or line tubes radius 0.012–0.016 connecting every nearest-neighbor pair separated by one lattice spacing along exactly one local axis; total 54 rods per lattice. Front layer is local z = -1, middle layer z = 0, back layer z = +1. Left panel {100}: draw one square teal plane at local z = 0, corners (-1,-1,0), (1,-1,0), (1,1,0), (-1,1,0), parallel to the front/back cube faces and passing through the 9 middle-sheet atoms. Right panel {110}: draw multiple parallel diagonal planes with equations x - z = c for c = -1, 0, +1, each clipped to the cube bounds -1 ≤ x,y,z ≤ 1. These vertical diagonal planes should run visually from the lower-left/front side toward the upper-right/receding side of the cube in the same perspective view. The central c = 0 plane passes through atoms (-1,y,-1), (0,y,0), and (1,y,1); the c = +1 and c = -1 planes pass through the adjacent parallel diagonal atom rows where integer coordinates satisfy x - z = ±1. Teal planes should be pale and translucent, not saturated: base color #9fd3d0 with alpha about 0.20–0.26. To match the source, split each plane into a slightly darker interior/lower portion, color #78bcbc alpha about 0.28–0.34, and a paler upper/exposed strip, color #c3e7e2 alpha about 0.14–0.20. Avoid thick outlines on the teal planes in source-faithful mode. If measurementAids is true, show unobtrusive arrows and labels outside the cube: d100 = a = 1 between adjacent z-parallel planes, and d110 = a/√2 ≈ 0.707 along the unit normal (1,0,-1)/√2 between adjacent x - z = c planes. If measurementAids is false, hide all spacing arrows, text labels, halos, and atom highlights so the display is source-faithful.
plan.notes: Default layoutMode must render both panels simultaneously, side by side, rather than replacing one with the other. In Single lattice mode, center one lattice and use focusedFamily to switch between the {100} plane and the full {110} set of parallel planes. For the {110} family, do not replace the parallel planes with only one active plane or a dashed outline; render the visible clipped translucent planes at c = -1, 0, +1 together. Render rods first, translucent planes next with double-sided material, depthTest enabled and depthWrite disabled, then atoms last so red spheres remain crisp on top of the pale teal sheets. Keep source-faithful mode visually clean: no captions inside the scene, no glowing atom halos, no dashed spacing outlines, and no arrows unless measurementAids is enabled. Orbit should rotate both side-by-side lattice groups together in Source comparison mode so the comparison remains aligned.

authoredPrompt: This figure shows two identical cubic crystal lattices drawn side by side in perspective. Each is a three-by-three-by-three array of small red spheres standing for atoms, joined by thin black lines tracing the cube edges and the rows between nearest neighbors, so the block reads as open and transparent. In the left lattice, a translucent teal plane lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the middle sheet of atoms, appearing darker where it sits behind the front layer of spheres and paler where it emerges near the top face. In the right lattice, the highlighted plane is tilted instead, slicing diagonally from the lower left of the cube toward the upper right and intersecting a different set of spheres, its shading again splitting between a darker interior portion and a lighter one near the top. Holding the lattice fixed while changing only the orientation of the shaded plane makes that orientation the single variable in view. The pair conveys that one crystal holds many families of parallel atomic planes at differing angles and spacings, each able to produce its own X-ray diffraction.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between plane families: the learner switches named plane orientations, the teal plane moves from face-parallel to diagonal cuts through the same red-sphere lattice, showing that one crystal contains multiple families of atomic planes.
- Slider for plane spacing index: the learner steps through adjacent parallel planes in the selected family, successive translucent sheets highlight different rows of atoms and the spacing label updates, connecting plane orientation and spacing to diffraction conditions.
authoredContext:
Although the figure depicts a crystal as a two-dimensional array of scattering centers for simplicity, real crystals are structures in three dimensions. Scattering can occur simultaneously from different families of planes at different orientations and spacing patterns known as called Bragg planes, as shown in the figure. The resulting interference pattern can be quite complex.

Because of the regularity that makes a crystal structure, one crystal can have many families of planes within its geometry, each one giving rise to X-ray diffraction.

Figure shows two crystal lattices, with atoms shown as small circles, connected to each other by lines. In the first lattice, flat planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In the second, slanted planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In each case, the planes are seen as a combination of different atoms in the same lattice.

interactions.label: Plane family
interactions.teaches: The same cubic crystal contains multiple families of parallel atomic planes; changing the family changes both the orientation of the sheet and the diffraction-relevant spacing.

interactions.label: Plane index
interactions.teaches: Adjacent planes in one family are parallel copies separated by a fixed distance, so diffraction depends on the family spacing rather than on one isolated sheet.
Rotating the lattice makes clear that the teal patch is a flat plane cutting through a three-dimensional array of atoms, not just a colored region on the drawing.

demo_steps.title: Face-parallel plane
demo_steps.narration: The highlighted {100} plane is parallel to the front and back cube faces. It passes through a complete square sheet of atoms inside the same cubic lattice.

demo_steps.title: Adjacent face-parallel plane
demo_steps.narration: Moving the index shifts the teal sheet to the next parallel layer of atoms. The orientation stays fixed and the spacing label remains d100 = a.

demo_steps.title: Diagonal plane family
demo_steps.narration: Switching to {110} keeps the same red-sphere lattice but tilts the teal plane diagonally through it, matching the right-hand panel of the source figure.

demo_steps.title: Adjacent diagonal plane
demo_steps.narration: The next diagonal sheet is parallel to the first but closer than the face-parallel planes. The spacing label changes to d110 = a/√2.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use an oblique crystal drawing: +X is screen-right, +Y is screen-up, and +Z is the receding diagonal up and to the right. The cube is 3 × 3 × 3 world units with lattice points at integer coordinates x,y,z ∈ {0,1,2,3}; lattice spacing a = 1. The front face z = 0 should read as an undistorted square with horizontal and vertical grid lines, while depth lines recede diagonally. Red atom spheres radius about 0.085–0.11 units, glossy red #d71920 with small white specular highlight and darker red underside. Black rods radius about 0.012–0.018 units, color #111111, drawn between every nearest-neighbor pair separated by one lattice spacing along exactly one axis. The {100} face-parallel plane should match the left source panel: a square sheet parallel to the front/back cube faces, normal along +Z, with corners (0,0,z0), (3,0,z0), (3,3,z0), (0,3,z0), where z0 = planeIndex - 1. Default planeIndex 2 gives z0 = 1, a middle sheet behind the front layer of atoms. The {110} diagonal plane should match the right source panel: a vertical diagonal sheet with normal proportional to (1,0,-1), using x - z = c where c = planeIndex - 2. Default planeIndex 2 gives x = z, running from the lower-left/front side toward the upper-right/receding side in screen space. For each family, compute the visible teal polygon by clipping the mathematical plane to the cube bounds 0 ≤ x,y,z ≤ 3. Active plane color translucent teal #6fb8b8 at alpha 0.42; use a paler top/far overlap #b8dddd at alpha 0.28 if splitting the polygon helps mimic the source's lighter and darker regions. Highlight atoms whose plane equation is satisfied within tolerance 0.02. Spacing formulas for cubic lattice: d100 = a = 1 and d110 = a/√2 ≈ 0.707. Draw the spacing arrow along the corresponding unit normal between the active sheet and the adjacent sheet; keep the label near the arrow but offset outside the cube so it does not hide atom rows.
interactionPlan.notes: Do not display the two textbook panels side by side initially; use the family toggle to replace the left-panel plane with the right-panel diagonal plane in the same fixed lattice. Render rods before spheres so atoms sit visually on top of intersections. Use double-sided transparent material for the teal plane, with depthWrite disabled and depthTest enabled to preserve the source-like sense that red atoms and black grid lines remain visible through the sheet. Plane polygons can be generated by intersecting the selected plane equation with the twelve cube edges, sorting the resulting vertices around their centroid, and triangulating as a fan. Text labels should be CSS2D or sprite labels that stay readable during orbit.

discrepancies: The source shows two lattice panels side by side, while the generated figure shows only one lattice at a time and relies on controls for the second case.

The right-hand source panel shows multiple translucent parallel diagonal planes, but the generated {110} mode appears to use one filled plane plus a dashed adjacent outline rather than the same stack of shaded planes.
The generated figure adds spacing arrows and labels such as d100 = a and {100} plane family, which are not present in the source figure.
Highlighted atom halos and brighter selected atoms are added on the active plane, making the lattice visually busier than the source.
The generated plane annotation and UI emphasize crystallographic indexing more than the original, which is a clean unlabeled visual comparison.
evaluation.notes: The cubic lattice, red atoms, black rods, and translucent plane idea are recognizable, but the generated figure adds annotations and does not closely reproduce the two-panel source composition or the multi-plane diagonal view.

discrepancies: The right {110} panel's translucent planes are rendered as several clipped sheets with uneven visible overlap, while the source shows cleaner, broad parallel diagonal bands.

The left shaded {100} plane appears slightly too centered and uniformly translucent compared with the source, where the plane visually reads more like a single face-parallel slab with stronger depth occlusion.
The generated atoms are glossy spheres with bright specular highlights, whereas the source uses simpler red nodes with subtler shading.
The generated lattice rods are slightly thicker and denser-looking than the source, making the grid visually heavier.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is clearly recognizable as the same two-panel cubic lattice plane comparison, with only minor differences in plane appearance, node styling, and grid weight.
action_items: Make the {110} planes visually cleaner and closer to the broad translucent diagonal bands in the source.
Reduce rod thickness slightly to better match the lighter black lattice lines of the original.
Tone down atom gloss/highlights for a closer textbook-style red-node appearance.
Adjust the {100} plane opacity and placement so it reads more like the source's single face-parallel internal slab.
